analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for bank regulators to overturn consumer financial rules and replaces the bureau's single director.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 241-173 on July 21, 2011, but the Senate Banking Committee never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten part of the 2010 Dodd-Frank law so that a simple majority of bank regulators on the Financial Stability Oversight Council — instead of a two-thirds vote under a stricter test — could overturn any Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rule. It also would have replaced the consumer bureau's single director with a five-member commission and delayed the transfer of consumer-protection powers until a chair was confirmed. A second title would have terminated the FHA Short Refinance program for underwater homeowners and canceled its unspent funds.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, mortgage lenders, and other financial companies. Under the bill, any agency on the Financial Stability Oversight Council could petition to void a consumer bureau rule, and the council would be required to set it aside on a simple majority vote whenever it found the rule "inconsistent with the safe and sound operations" of financial institutions — a far easier test than the current requirement that the rule put the banking system at risk. Financial firms also benefited from Title II, which ended the FHA Short Refinance program that had relied on lenders and investors writing down loan balances for underwater borrowers.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the vote needed for the Financial Stability Oversight Council to stay or overturn a consumer bureau rule from two-thirds to a simple majority, and changes the standard from a rule that would "put the safety and soundness of the U.S. banking system... at risk" to one that is merely "inconsistent with the safe and sound operations" of financial institutions — making it far easier to void consumer rules.

Requires the council to set aside a consumer bureau rule whenever a member agency petitions and finds it inconsistent with financial institutions' safe and sound operations, and lets petitions be filed on any subject regardless of the agency's expertise; it also removes deadlines that previously forced dismissal of petitions.

Replaces the consumer bureau's single director with a five-member commission and delays the transfer of consumer-protection powers to the bureau until a commission chair is confirmed by the Senate — the structure the financial industry had sought since Dodd-Frank passed.

Terminates the FHA Short Refinance program, voids the HUD mortgagee letter that created it, and rescinds its unexpended funds to the Treasury for debt reduction, ending a program that required lenders and investors to forgive part of the loan balance on underwater mortgages.

Adds accountability provisions supporters pointed to: council meetings on rule overrides must be open and livestreamed, council members cannot vote if they worked for a regulated company in the prior two years, the bureau must publish detailed spending and rule lists, and each new rule must be analyzed for its financial impact and its effect on access to credit.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and underwater homeowners. A weakened override process and a lower standard would make it easier for banking regulators to strike down consumer bureau rules covering mortgages, foreclosures, credit cards, and debt collection. The five-member commission, with Senate confirmations required and the transfer of powers delayed until a chair was confirmed, would have slowed the bureau's ability to write and enforce rules. Title II eliminated the FHA Short Refinance option for homeowners who owed more than their homes were worth, leaving a website notice directing struggling borrowers to contact their member of Congress.

drawbacks.text: The core change would have made consumer protections much easier to erase: a mandatory set-aside on a simple majority vote, using a standard keyed to financial institutions' convenience rather than system-wide risk, would give banking regulators a standing tool to block bureau rules on mortgages, foreclosures, credit cards, and debt collection.

Replacing the single director with a five-member commission requiring Senate confirmation, and delaying the transfer of consumer-protection powers until a chair was confirmed, would have slowed or frozen the bureau's work — the same commission structure used to leave other agencies gridlocked during confirmation fights.

Ending the FHA Short Refinance program removed one of the few refinancing paths for borrowers who owed more on their mortgages than their homes were worth during the foreclosure crisis, replacing it with a HUD website notice telling borrowers to ask their member of Congress for help negotiating with their lender.

Supporters' strongest good-faith points: concentrating sweeping rulemaking and enforcement power in one unelected director had drawn legitimate concern, and a commission mirrors the structure of the FDIC and FTC; the FHA program was voluntary and had limited reach, and its unspent funds would go to debt reduction. The bill itself directed HUD to study how much the program was actually used.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's genuine accountability features — livestreamed council meetings, a two-year conflict-of-interest voting ban, published bureau spending, and required analyses of rules' impact on credit access — are modest bookkeeping next to its central effect. The heart of the bill was to lower the bar for bank regulators to void consumer bureau rules and to break the bureau's leadership into a commission that could be stalled by confirmation fights, while also canceling a refinancing program for underwater homeowners. For consumers, the costs would have outweighed the added transparency.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it in July 2011, but the Senate Banking Committee never took it up, and the bill died when that Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Sean Duffy introduced the bill on April 1, 2011, after subcommittee hearings held even before its introduction and referral.
The subcommittee forwarded it 13-9 and the House Financial Services Committee ordered it reported 35-22; the committee reported an amended bill on May 25, 2011.

The House debated it under a rule on July 21, 2011; a motion to recommit that would have preserved the two-thirds vote for overturning rules protecting seniors from foreclosure, robosigning, reverse-mortgage, and retirement-savings fraud failed 183-232, with 182 of 193 Democrats in favor and 231 of 239 Republicans opposed.

The House passed the bill 241-173: 231 of 239 Republicans voted yes against just 10 of 193 Democrats, while 172 Democrats and 1 Republican voted no. The text of H.R. 830, terminating the FHA Refinance Program, was appended to the bill.

The Senate received the bill on July 22, 2011, and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, which took no further action; it never received a Senate vote and died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers came out ahead: because the Senate never acted, the consumer bureau kept its single director, its rules kept the two-thirds override protection, and the FHA Short Refinance program was not terminated.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers; consumer bureau rules stayed intact

for.name: Rep. Sean Duffy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through the House.

for.name: House Financial Services Committee
for.role: Reported the bill 35-22 after subcommittee approval 13-9
for.what_they_did: Marked up and reported the amended bill to the House floor.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred on July 22, 2011; the bill never reached the Senate floor.

against.name: Rep. Mike Michaud
against.what_they_did: Offered a motion to recommit that would have kept the two-thirds vote requirement for overturning rules protecting seniors from foreclosure, robosigning, reverse-mortgage, and retirement-savings fraud; it failed 183-232.

against.name: Obama administration
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the bill, with the president's senior advisers stating they would recommend a veto if it reached his desk.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split sharply by party: 231 of 239 Republicans voted yes while only 10 of 193 Democrats joined them, and 172 Democrats and 1 Republican voted no; a motion to recommit failed along nearly the same lines at 183-232.

industries.industry: Banks and other regulated financial institutions
industries.note: The bill would have let a simple majority of bank regulators on the oversight council void any consumer bureau rule under a standard focused on institutions' own 'safe and sound operations' rather than system-wide risk, giving the industry a routine path to strike down rules on mortgages, credit cards, and debt collection.

Title II terminated the FHA Short Refinance program, which had relied on lenders and investors writing down balances for underwater borrowers, and replaced it with a notice telling struggling homeowners to contact Congress for help negotiating with their lender or servicer.

The bureau's head would have been replaced by a five-member commission requiring Senate confirmation, the transfer of its powers delayed until a chair was confirmed, and its rules made far easier for other regulators to override; it would also have faced new analysis and reporting requirements.
